The regional airport authority has spent the past three years planning the largest overhaul of the terminal since it opened in 1978. The project began as a modest plan to replace the aging baggage belts, but successive reviews widened its scope until it touched nearly every part of the building. Engineers say the existing structure, built when the airport handled fewer than two million travellers a year, can no longer absorb the summer peaks that now push the terminal past its design capacity for weeks at a time.

The first phase, already under way, has moved check-in desks into a temporary hall beside the short-stay car park while workers rebuild the floor above. A light-rail spur will connect the arrivals level to the city's central station, and a covered walkway will link the new platform to the rental counters. The redesign also folds in a larger security hall, additional gates on the eastern pier, and a consolidated baggage hall with self-service drop-off kiosks.

Community meetings this spring drew residents from the neighbourhoods under the flight path, many of whom asked about noise, night-time construction and the future of the older warehouses along the perimeter road. The authority's planning director said the consultation had changed several details, including the routing of the service road and the height of the screening wall near the primary school. Local councillors pressed for a commitment to apprenticeships, and the authority agreed to reserve a share of the construction jobs for residents of the surrounding boroughs. The authority also published a noise contour map showing that the loudest departures would shift east once the new pier opened.

Financing has been the harder question. The authority's reserves were depleted during the years when passenger numbers collapsed, and the remaining debt from the 2009 refurbishment is still being serviced. A mixture of borrowing, a passenger facility charge and a one-off grant from the regional transport fund makes up the package. Rates on the authority's existing bonds have risen since the summer, and the finance director warned that any further increase would push the annual debt service above the level assumed in the plan. Officials have said the project will be delivered in stages so that the borrowing can be refinanced if interest rates fall.

At its meeting on Tuesday, the authority's board approved the terminal expansion at an estimated cost of 1.2 billion, financed through a mix of bonds and federal grants. Work on the second phase is expected to begin in the autumn, and the authority has promised that the terminal will remain open throughout.
